The Kessler Arena opens at five-thirty on Saturday mornings, and for most of last winter I was the person who unlocked it. My job was simple: sweep the bleachers, switch on the overhead lights one row at a time, and stay out of the way of Mrs. Petrakis, who drove the resurfacing machine and had driven it since before my mother learned to skate.

The machine was a squat green thing that looked like a tractor wearing a box. Mrs. Petrakis drove it in slow, overlapping ovals, shaving the scarred surface and laying a thin sheet of hot water behind her. She kept her eyes on the boards the whole time, as if reading something written along the bottom of them. I could have watched her for hours, and some mornings I nearly did.

One morning in February the Ridgefield coach, a tall man named Mr. Drummond, arrived forty minutes early with his whole team. They had a tournament that afternoon, and he wanted extra practice. He walked straight to the gate and told Mrs. Petrakis to open it as soon as she had made her last pass.

She shut off the engine and climbed down. Fresh water, she explained, needs ten minutes to freeze all the way through. A skater who steps on it sooner leaves ruts that harden into the surface, and the next player to catch an edge in one of those ruts goes down hard. Mr. Drummond said his players were careful, and that ten minutes was a long time to stand around in skates.

Mrs. Petrakis looked at the clock above the scoreboard. Then she sat down on the bench beside the gate, folded her hands on her knees, and waited. Mr. Drummond paced. A few of his players laughed nervously and then went quiet. I stood by the light switches and tried to look busy.

At exactly the tenth minute she stood, pressed her thumb against the ice near the gate, and swung the gate open. The team poured out. That afternoon, I heard later, Ridgefield won its tournament on a goal scored in the final minute by a defenseman who kept his feet through a collision at the blue line.

I asked her afterward whether she had been concerned that Mr. Drummond would complain to the manager. She shrugged and said that coaches came and went, but the ice was hers every morning. I have repeated that answer to myself many times since, usually when someone is asking me to hurry something that should take as long as it takes.

The summer I was twelve, I decided to make my fortune in eggs. I had done the arithmetic on the back of a cereal box: six hens, one egg each per day, sold to the neighbors at fifty cents apiece, came to a figure that would buy me a telescope by Labor Day. I presented the plan to my parents at dinner, along with a chart I had colored in with markers.

My father asked where the hens would live. I had an answer ready: the old tool shed behind the garage, which needed only a door that closed properly and some straw. My mother asked who would feed them in August, when we visited my aunt. I said I would teach my brother, who was seven and had once kept a goldfish alive for nearly a month.

To my astonishment, they agreed. My grandfather drove me to a farm two towns over, where a woman in rubber boots sold me six young hens out of a wire pen and gave me advice I wrote on my hand in ballpoint. I named the hens after the planets, skipping Earth because it seemed unlucky, and installed them in the shed with a bucket of feed and a water dish I had borrowed from the dog.

For three weeks the planets laid nothing. I checked the straw every morning and every evening and found only straw and, once, a very surprised toad. When I telephoned the woman in the rubber boots, she explained that young hens begin laying when they are ready, and that a chart has very little influence on them.

The first egg, when it finally came, was the size of a walnut. I carried it into the kitchen in both hands, as though it might hatch on the way. By September I had sold eleven eggs, most of them to my grandmother, who paid a dollar each and said they were the best she had ever tasted. The telescope stayed in the catalog.

I still have the chart. The line for my profits climbs so steeply that it runs off the top of the poster board and continues onto a strip of paper taped above it. Saturn, the last of the six, lived another nine years and never once laid an egg on a weekend.

For forty years there were eleven wooden benches on Front Street in Marlow, one outside nearly every shop between the post office and the river. Last spring the town council removed them. In their place it installed a row of slanted metal rails, about hip height, that a person can lean against for a minute or two but cannot comfortably sit on.

The council's reasons were printed in the Marlow Ledger. Benches, the statement said, encouraged loitering, collected litter, and needed repainting every few years. The rails would keep foot traffic moving past the shop windows, which is good for business, and would last for decades with almost no upkeep.

Each of those claims deserves a closer look. The litter on Front Street comes mostly from the takeout counters, and it now blows along the sidewalk instead of gathering beside the benches, where the cleaning crew used to find it in one place. The repainting cost the town roughly six hundred dollars a year, less than it spent on the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rails. As for loitering, that word deserves a closer look too.

The people who used the benches most were Mr. Abernathy, who is eighty-four and walks to the pharmacy in two stages; parents waiting for the school bus with toddlers on their laps; the woman from the hardware store who ate her lunch outside on fine days; and teenagers trading gossip after school. These are the people who make a street feel occupied, and an occupied street is a safer and friendlier one than an empty street with tidy rails.

It is true that the rails keep people moving. That is precisely the trouble. A town center is valuable because people stop in it: they run into neighbors, they notice a new window display, they decide on the spot to buy a coffee. A shopper with nowhere to rest will finish her errand and drive home. Several shop owners on Front Street told me their afternoon trade has fallen since the spring, though they asked me to leave their names out.

The council meets again in October. Bringing back a few of the benches would cost very little, and the old ones are still stacked in the public works yard behind the fire station. A town that wants people on its main street should give them somewhere to sit.

Food arrives in small amounts: bits of leaves and insects washed down from the surface, and the droppings of a colony of bats that roosts near the entrance. At that rate, the colony could vanish within the lifetime of the animals now living in it.

Some caution is needed with such numbers. Cave animals are difficult to count, and a single survey can miss animals sheltering in cracks too narrow for a person to reach. The bats face pressures of their own, and fewer bats would mean less food in the pools whatever happens on the ridge. Still, every measurement points the same way.

What makes the decline hard to reverse is the salamander's own slow pace. A female may lay eggs only once every few years, and the young take more than a decade to mature.
